source.title: Decode-gLM: Tools to Interpret, Audit, and Steer Genomic Language Models
source.authors: Aaron Maiwald; Piotr Jedryszek; Florent Draye; B. Schölkopf; Garrett M. Morris; O. Crook

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE methods recover biological features in genomic language models, extending feature-recovery evidence to a new model setting; it does not test the original toy-network geometry.
record.gate_note: Included SAE feature-recovery and probing results bearing on V4. The steering results are not rows for these versions: the model is deliberately steered, and the reported outcome is a prediction shift rather than a measure of spontaneous feature representation. Contamination matches and sequence-ablation results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains overcomplete SAEs on a pretrained transformer language model over DNA (Nucleotide Transformer). It reports how many sparse, annotation-matching features the SAEs recover, compared with the model's own MLP neurons. That bears on V4 (sparse features a dictionary can recover) in a new setting, genomic rather than text LMs. It does not test toy models, capacity, geometry or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAEs on the Nucleotide Transformer recover over 100 interpretable biological annotations, can audit training data (CMV contamination), reveal hierarchies via meta-SAEs, and steer predictions. They frame their central hypothesis as gLM activations encoding biological properties 'in superposition'. However, they do not test superposition directly beyond SAE latents being more interpretable than neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses overcomplete BatchTopK SAEs and annotation-based feature evaluation on pretrained genomic language models, rather than training controlled toy networks with synthetic features and measuring superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of interpretable latents varies strongly by layer: none were found at the first layer of the 50m model and the count peaked at the seventh layer with over 60. The 500m model was evaluated only at layer 10.

fits_no_version.finding: A meta-SAE trained on SAE decoder weights finds a latent grouping several HIV-related SAE features. Used as a probe, it scores F1 57.2% on the combined set versus ≤44.8% for any single annotation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in a genomic LM are organised hierarchically, with more abstract meta-features composed of finer SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on pretrained MLP outputs beat probes on a randomly initialised model by at least 17.2 F1 points, and by over 50 on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The concepts recovered by the SAE are linearly encoded because of pretraining, not because of architecture alone.

record.problems: The study uses plasmids with functional annotations rather than the model's pretraining distribution; results vary by layer; the 500m model is tested only at layer 10; most reported feature metrics have no uncertainty estimates in the text; the paper does not establish feature completeness or stability.
record.rows_left_out: Steering outcomes in §2.4 and Figure 4 were left out because steering deliberately induces prediction changes rather than measuring spontaneous feature representation. BLAST contamination findings and sequence-ablation results in §2.2 and Supplementary §C.1 do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No toy networks, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No direct measure of how many neurons each feature spans. Superposition is inferred from SAE latents beating MLP neurons. Only one architecture family is tested, on off-distribution plasmid data.
No completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicity tests. The meta-SAE hierarchy is reported but not framed as evidence against canonical units.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Standard-F1 versus domain-F1 comparison for SAE latents. Domain recall inflates F1, and only some latents stay high under the standard metric.
SAE quality metrics: dead latents of 36–78% in most SAEs (77.72% for 500m) and NMSE of 0.0075–0.118. These are needed to judge how many dictionary features are actually recovered.
Per-layer counts of interpretable SAE latents versus MLP neurons, and F1 distributions. These are given only in the figure.

record.verdict_notes: V4 names LLMs. A genomic masked-language transformer is treated here as the same kind of system, so this is a new-setting test (T3). Steering results are correctly left out. Note that steering specificity collapses out of distribution, with non-AMR latents also shifting rank, which could matter for any later claim about SAE features as causal units. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity alone evidences superposition.
Tests SAE feature recovery in genomic language models, not whether features are spread across many neurons in general-purpose LLMs.
Does not establish SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Nucleotide Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Reported the CMV-enhancer representation's F1-score in discussing the amount of matching contamination.
rows.note: The paper separately reports 59% for a CMV-enhancer SAE-latent in §2.1; the measure or evaluation distinction behind the two figures is not clarified in the text.
rows.check: The 78% is described only as the model's 'CMV enhancer representation' in §2.2. The context suggests a linear-probe score rather than an SAE latent; §2.1 gives the SAE latent 59%. It cannot be read as an SAE-recovery value.

rows.subject: Nucleotide Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared logistic-regression probes on MLP outputs from pretrained and randomly initialised models.
rows.value: The smallest increase was an absolute 17.2%; the average increase was over 50%.
rows.note: The text reports these increases across probes but does not provide the individual values or map them to each model-layer condition.
rows.check: Linear probes on raw MLP outputs, pretrained vs random init. This is a control showing the concepts are learned in pretraining. It measures neither sparse dictionary recovery nor spreading across neurons, and no SAE was trained on the random model.

rows.subject: Nucleotide Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the encoder row for meta-SAE latent #107 as a linear classifier for HIV-related annotations.
rows.baseline: Any individual annotation or subset tested; no individual annotation exceeded 44.8%.
rows.value: 57.2% for the combined set of HIV-related annotations
rows.note: The meta-SAE latent captures a combined annotation group, rather than a single annotation.
rows.check: The meta-SAE is trained on SAE decoder weights, not model activations. The result concerns hierarchical grouping of features, not whether the model holds SAE-recoverable sparse features. It may bear loosely on V5 canonicity, but the study does not frame or test it that way.

relationships.condition: 50m model at middle/late layers (4, 7, 10, 12) and 500m model at layer 10, plasmid inputs
relationships.reason: Interpretable SAE latents (F1≥20%) far outnumber interpretable MLP neurons and score higher: over 60 at layer 7, and 135 latent-concept pairs in the 500m model, with top F1 up to 87.3% (R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Interpretable SAE latents (F1 of at least 20%) far outnumbered and outscored interpretable MLP neurons, with over 60 at layer 7 and 135 latent-concept pairs in the 500m model. Top F1 reached 87.3%.

relationships.condition: First MLP layer of the 50m model
relationships.reason: No SAE latent reached the F1≥20% threshold at layer 1, so recoverable features depend strongly on depth (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: No SAE latent reached an F1 of 20% or more at layer 1, so recoverable features depend strongly on depth.

relationships.condition: Choice of evaluation metric (domain F1 vs standard F1); from text, not rows
relationships.reason: Methods B.3 say domain recall 'significantly increases' F1 and standard F1 values are generally lower. Feature-recovery counts depend on the metric, and the interpretability threshold is low (20%). Based on the text; no row records this.
relationships.display_finding: The methods say domain recall 'significantly increases' F1 and that standard F1 values are generally lower. The number of recovered features therefore depends on the metric, and the 20% interpretability threshold is low.
